# 📖🗣️ Notable Events
## 293 replies
1471 - King Henry VI of England dies in the Tower of London, likely murdered on orders from King Edward IV, marking a significant event in the 'Wars of the Roses.'
1527 - King Philip II of Spain, one of the most powerful monarchs in European history, is born.
1765 - Windsor Agricultural Fair [North America's oldest] is founded, in Windsor, Nova Scotia.
1819 - The first bicycles, called 'swift walkers,' are introduced in the U.S.
1851 - The Herndon Expedition departs Lima, Peru, beginning a significant exploration of the Amazon basin to determine its navigability.
1881 - Clara Barton establishes the 'American Red Cross,' in Washington, D.C.
1901 - The first U.S. speed limit law for motor vehicles [12 mph in the city/15 mph in the country] is passed, in Connecticut.
1904 - The Fédération Internationale de Football Association [FIFA], the world governing body of association football, is founded, in Paris.
1908 - 'Dr. Jekyll & Mr. Hyde' premieres in Chicago and is the first horror movie in the U.S.
1918 - During World War I, Ensign Daniel A. J. Sullivan risks his life to secure depth charges on the converted yacht Christabel, saving his ship and earning the Medal of Honor.
1927 - Charles Lindbergh completes the first solo nonstop transatlantic flight, landing in Paris after departing from New York the previous day.
1932 - Amelia Earhart becomes the first woman to fly solo nonstop across the Atlantic Ocean.
1934 - The first municipality in the U.S. to fingerprint all of its citizens takes place, in Oskaloosa, Iowa.
1939 - Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini sign the 'Pact of Steel,' a military and political alliance between Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy.
1941 - The U.S. freighter Robin Moor, clearly marked with U.S. flags, is torpedoed and sunk by a German U-boat, marking the first sinking of an American merchant ship during World War II.

# 📖🗣️ Notable Events
## 293 replies
1944 - A large explosion aboard the USS LST-353 at Pearl Harbor naval base sets off a chain reaction, sinking six LSTs and killing 163 men.
[This incident was classified 'top secret,' until 1960.]
1945 - Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall are married.
1951 - The influential '9th Street Show' opens in New York.
[Often considered the birth of the New York School of abstract expressionism.]
1968 - The nuclear-powered submarine USS Scorpion [SSN-589] sinks 400 miles southwest of the Azores Islands, with the loss of all 99 crew members.
1972 - Michelangelo's Pietà statue is attacked with a hammer by a man screaming, 'I am Jesus Christ! I have risen from the dead!'
1979 - Violent clashes, known as the 'White Night Riots,' erupt in San Francisco after a lenient sentencing for Harvey Milk's murderer, Dan White.
1980 - Star Wars Episode V: 'The Empire Strikes Back' is released in theaters.
1980 - Ensign Jean Marie Butler and 13 other women become the first women to graduate from the U.S. Coast Guard Academy.
1980 - President Jimmy Carter declares a state of emergency at Love Canal in Niagara Falls, New York, due to a toxic dumping site.
1985 - Patti Frustaci gives birth to the first septuplets in the United States.
1991 - Rajiv Gandhi, former Prime Minister of India, is assassinated by a suicide bomber.
1992 - The first episode of 'The Real World' airs on MTV.
1992 - The final episode of 'MacGyver' airs on ABC.
[The final episode of the original 'MacGyver' series aired on April 25, 1992, on ABC. While a previously unaired episode was shown on May 21, 1992, that was intended to be the finale.]

1992 - Mrithi, the Rwandan mountain gorilla featured in 'Gorillas in the Mist,' is shot and killed by a government patrol during the Rwandan war.
1999 - Actress Susan Lucci finally wins a Daytime Emmy Award for her role as Erica Kane on 'All My Children,' after 18 previous nominations.
2005 - 'Kingda Ka,' the world's tallest roller coaster, opens at 'Six Flags Great Adventure,' in New Jersey.
2008 - Lou Pearlman, music mogul behind the 'Backstreet Boys,' and 'NSYNC,' is sentenced to 25 years in prison for a multi-decade scam.
2011 - Radio broadcaster Harold Camping's prediction of the world ending on this day does not come to pass.
2017 - The Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey Circus perform their final show at the Nassau Veterans Memorial Coliseum, in Uniondale, New York.

# 📖🗣️ Notable Events
## 293 replies
1471 - King Henry VI of England dies in the Tower of London, likely murdered on orders from King Edward IV, marking a significant event in the 'Wars of the Roses.'
1527 - King Philip II of Spain, one of the most powerful monarchs in European history, is born.
1765 - Windsor Agricultural Fair [North America's oldest] is founded, in Windsor, Nova Scotia.
1819 - The first bicycles, called 'swift walkers,' are introduced in the U.S.
1851 - The Herndon Expedition departs Lima, Peru, beginning a significant exploration of the Amazon basin to determine its navigability.
1881 - Clara Barton establishes the 'American Red Cross,' in Washington, D.C.
1901 - The first U.S. speed limit law for motor vehicles [12 mph in the city/15 mph in the country] is passed, in Connecticut.
1904 - The Fédération Internationale de Football Association [FIFA], the world governing body of association football, is founded, in Paris.
1908 - 'Dr. Jekyll & Mr. Hyde' premieres in Chicago and is the first horror movie in the U.S.
1918 - During World War I, Ensign Daniel A. J. Sullivan risks his life to secure depth charges on the converted yacht Christabel, saving his ship and earning the Medal of Honor.
1927 - Charles Lindbergh completes the first solo nonstop transatlantic flight, landing in Paris after departing from New York the previous day.
1932 - Amelia Earhart becomes the first woman to fly solo nonstop across the Atlantic Ocean.
1934 - The first municipality in the U.S. to fingerprint all of its citizens takes place, in Oskaloosa, Iowa.
1939 - Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini sign the 'Pact of Steel,' a military and political alliance between Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy.
1941 - The U.S. freighter Robin Moor, clearly marked with U.S. flags, is torpedoed and sunk by a German U-boat, marking the first sinking of an American merchant ship during World War II.

## [PDF page 11]
One of the diseases that has yet to be eradicated in the INDOPACOM is malaria. Malaria is an ancient parasit-  
ic disease caused by the presence of various Plasmodium species in the blood. The common vector is the fe-  
male Anopheles mosquito. The disease is very debilitating, often resulting in death. A common early treatment  
(dating to the 17th Century) consisted of preparations made from the bark of the Cinchona tree. Further refine-  
ment during 1800s produced quinine, which could be given in standardized doses by mouth for the prevention  
and control of the disease or in an injectable form for treatment of severe cases beginning in the 1890s.  
Malaria was endemic in the U.S., especially the South, even into the 20th Century. It affected military  
strength during the Civil War, and again became a major issue during the Spanish-American War in 1898. At  
the end of this brief conflict America became a global power, acquiring several new overseas territories, in-  
cluding the Philippine Islands and the Marianas. The importance in controlling and treating this illness contin-  
ued for America during the 20th century due to World War II and the Vietnam War. Given America’s extend-  
ed presence in the area, the AMEDD Museum has a variety of objects in its collection relating to the ongoing  
battle with malaria.  
The AMEDD’s strategy for combatting malaria in the 20th Century not only included pharmaceutical  
interventions, but also preventive health measures. Among the preventative protocols were the use of mosquito  
netting (especially over beds and over hats); wire screens on windows; and drainage or spraying of stagnant  
water with oil. Quinine continued to be the preferred drug, including intravenous administration (in severe cas-  
es) for the prevention and control of malaria leading up to WWII. To inject quinine was a complex process as  
the tablets were first dissolved in sterile water, the mixture drawn into a syringe and then injected into the pa-  
tient. AMEDD medical officers stationed in the Philippines during and after WWI wore an officer’s medical  
belt that contained an assortment of pharmaceuticals, including a vial of quinine sulfate tablets for malaria,  
20mg.  

## [PDF page 11]
The main source of quinine by the end of the 19th Century was the Dutch East Indies (now Indonesia),  
and the world supply of quinine was largely under control of a consortium of growers which had banded to-  
gether to form the Kina Bureau, a cartel based in Amsterdam, which held an effective monopoly on this valua-  
ble medicinal. With the German invasion and occupation of the Netherlands in May 1940, they gained access  
to the warehouses and manufacturing capabilities of the Kina Bureau, putting most of the processed drug under  
Axis control. When Japanese forces overran the Dutch East Indies, in 1942, the raw supply of cinchona was  
lost to the Allies as well.  
While preventive measures, including spraying and the use of nets, continued, along with a campaign  
of informational printed material, a replacement had to be found for quinine. The drug initially selected to re-

## [PDF page 12]

place quinine was Atabrine (or Mepacrine), a drug first developed by Bayer in 1931. Atabrine was effective  
for malaria prevention and was issued to troops in endemic areas. One issue with atabrine was its profoundly  
bitter taste, even with the minimal contact involved with swallowing it.  
This caused non-compliance among the troops so that administration was often done at mealtime, with  
a medical officer observing to assure each dose was swallowed. Atabrine’s effect on the liver produced jaun-  
dice in patients taking it. Artist Franklin Boggs captured this unpleasant fact of daily life in the Army in a  
painting entitled “Pill Call.” Pacific veterans also believed that taking atabrine rendered one sterile, and the  
Japanese used that in propaganda to dissuade troops from taking atabrine.  
Captured Japanese medical supplies indicate that our  
adversary used both “Bagnon,” which was an intravenous  
treatment combining quinine, caffeine, and urethane as well as  
atabrine. A great breakthrough in eradication efforts came in  
1943 when the Army began using the chemical DDT to kill  
mosquitoes. Aerosol application of pyrethrins was also used to  
eradicate the mosquito.

One of the diseases that has yet to be eradicated in the INDOPACOM is malaria. Malaria is an ancient parasit-  
ic disease caused by the presence of various Plasmodium species in the blood. The common vector is the fe-  
male Anopheles mosquito. The disease is very debilitating, often resulting in death. A common early treatment  
(dating to the 17th Century) consisted of preparations made from the bark of the Cinchona tree. Further refine-  
ment during 1800s produced quinine, which could be given in standardized doses by mouth for the prevention  
and control of the disease or in an injectable form for treatment of severe cases beginning in the 1890s.  
Malaria was endemic in the U.S., especially the South, even into the 20th Century. It affected military  
strength during the Civil War, and again became a major issue during the Spanish-American War in 1898. At  
the end of this brief conflict America became a global power, acquiring several new overseas territories, in-  
cluding the Philippine Islands and the Marianas. The importance in controlling and treating this illness contin-  
ued for America during the 20th century due to World War II and the Vietnam War. Given America’s extend-  
ed presence in the area, the AMEDD Museum has a variety of objects in its collection relating to the ongoing  
battle with malaria.  
The AMEDD’s strategy for combatting malaria in the 20th Century not only included pharmaceutical  
interventions, but also preventive health measures. Among the preventative protocols were the use of mosquito  
netting (especially over beds and over hats); wire screens on windows; and drainage or spraying of stagnant  
water with oil. Quinine continued to be the preferred drug, including intravenous administration (in severe cas-  
es) for the prevention and control of malaria leading up to WWII. To inject quinine was a complex process as  
the tablets were first dissolved in sterile water, the mixture drawn into a syringe and then injected into the pa-  
tient. AMEDD medical officers stationed in the Philippines during and after WWI wore an officer’s medical  
belt that contained an assortment of pharmaceuticals, including a vial of quinine sulfate tablets for malaria,  
20mg.

and the world supply of quinine was largely under control of a consortium of growers which had banded to-

ble medicinal. With the German invasion and occupation of the Netherlands in May 1940, they gained access  
to the warehouses and manufacturing capabilities of the Kina Bureau, putting most of the processed drug under  
Axis control. When Japanese forces overran the Dutch East Indies, in 1942, the raw supply of cinchona was  
lost to the Allies as well.  
While preventive measures, including spraying and the use of nets, continued, along with a campaign

for malaria prevention and was issued to troops in endemic areas. One issue with atabrine was its profoundly  
bitter taste, even with the minimal contact involved with swallowing it.  
This caused non-compliance among the troops so that administration was often done at mealtime, with  
a medical officer observing to assure each dose was swallowed. Atabrine’s effect on the liver produced jaun-  
dice in patients taking it. Artist Franklin Boggs captured this unpleasant fact of daily life in the Army in a  
painting entitled “Pill Call.” Pacific veterans also believed that taking atabrine rendered one sterile, and the  
Japanese used that in propaganda to dissuade troops from taking atabrine.

atabrine. A great breakthrough in eradication efforts came in

mosquitoes. Aerosol application of pyrethrins was also used to  
eradicate the mosquito.

short.  (Poland,  normally  self-sufficient  in  grain,  pleaded  urgently  in  
November  for  the  delivery  of  500,000  tons  of  wheat.)  In  the  devastated  
areas  320,000  children  needed  total  care,  a  further  2,720,000  total  or  partial  
care.  In  rural  devastated  areas  154,000  rooms  were  urgently  required  to  
rebhouse  the  homeless—5  persons  to  a  room.  
Health  conditions  were  appalling.  Of  13,000  doctors  before  the  war,  
only  7,000  survive—one  to  3,500  persons.  Hospitals  were  stripped  bare  of  
all  equipment—beds,  bedding,  medicines,  surgical  supplies.  In  one  hos-  
pital  visited,  patients  suffering  from  contagious  diseases  lay  on  straw  piles  
covered  with  blankets,  threadbare  and  full  of  holes,  which,  perforce,  they  
had  brought  in  with  them.  One  patient,  desperately  sick,  was  seen  arriv-  
ing  on  a  horse-drawn  farm  cart.  She  had  travelled  30  miles  in  zero  weather  
lying  on  straw.  Spread  of  disease  continued  a  menace.  In  September  
alone,  there  were  over  16,000  notified  cases  of  typhoid.  Those  not  notified  
might  more  than  double  the  figure.  
To  such  needs UNRRA  brought  partial  relief.  Bedsteads,  mattresses  and  
blankets,  surgical  instruments  and  medicines  were  delivered in  subst:  ntial  
quantities.  Many  tons  of  DDT  powder  have  been  supplied.  Following  

## [PDF page 18]
an  exploratory  mission,  headed  by  UNRRA’s  chief  medical  officer,  a  
health  program,  growing  steadily  in  efficiency,  has  been  worked  out.  
But  the  crying  need,  of  both  the  sick  and  the  hale,  was  for  food,  and  food  
was  the  main  item  of  supply  during  a  quarter  in  which  shipments,  though  
still  short  of  the  need,  beat  all  previous  records.  
Cumulative  shipments,  through  December  31st,  totalled  348,200  gross  
long  tons,  of  which  200,000  tons  (or  nearly  60  percent)  were  shipped  
during  this  quarter.  The  previous  quarter’s  total  was  topped  by  over  
100  percent.  
But,  as  in  other  countries,  port  deliveries  did  not  mean  immediate  relief  
to  those  in  need.  Shortage  of  transportation  created  a  serious  bottleneck.  
In  mid-November  warehouses  in  the  port  of  Gdynia  were  over  60  percent  
full.  The  pipeline.of  supply  was  blocked  for  lack  of  freight  cars,  engines,  
trucks  to  carry  the  supplies  to  areas  of  acute  need.  The  shortage  affected  
not  only  the  delivery  of  supplies  from  abroad  but  distribution  of  food  
produced  within  the  country.  As  late  as  December,  three  million  tons  of  
coal  lay  stacked  at  Silesian  pitheads,  while  men  and  women  shivered  all  
across  the  country.  
By  the  end  of  the  year  some  headway  was  made.  4,800  vehicles  a  week  

## [PDF page 18]
were  being  shipped.  First  deliveries”  were  made  of  a  consignment  of  75  
locomotives  procured  for  Poland  from  U.  S.  Army  surpluses,  partial  answer  
to  congestion  at  Silesian  pitheads  and  similar  traffic  bottlenecks.  Enlarge  
ment  of  the  reception  capacity  at  the  ports  of  Gdynia  and  Gdansk  acceler-  
ated  shipment  to  some  100,000  tons  a  mouth  by  the  end  of  December.  It  
was  hoped  to  double  the  figure  by  February  1946.  
Substantial  help  came,  also,  with  delivery  of  15  million  pounds  of  clothing  
(12  million  pounds  contributed  by  voluntary  agencies  in  the  U.  S.).  Farm-

For  millions  the  life  of  man  continued  “solitary,  poor,  nasty,  brutish,

## [PDF page 21]
For  the  distress  in  China  differs  from  that  of  European  countries  only  
in  its  greater  extent  and  longer  incidence.  The  sufferings  of  a  continent  
are  here  comprised  within  a  single  nation  and  intensified,  despite  20  years  
of  rapid  progress  before  the  war,  by  limited  industrial  resources,  and  a  
transportation  system  which  lagged  far  behind  that  of  most  European  
countries.  Recovery  from  the  ravages  of  war  was,  therefore,  foredoomed  
to  be  slower  and  more  costly  in  human  lives  and  suffering.  
In  China  the  sight  of  men  and  women  visibly  dying  of  starvation  was  
common  over  wide  areas—despite  the  recent  gathering  of  the  harvest.  The  
sick,  the  homeless,  the  unemployed,  cry  out  for  help.  But  staggering  
obstacles  stand  in  the  way  of  its  provision.  
UNRRA  faced  its  first  problem  on  the  China  coast.  No  port  was  open  
to  relief  ships  until  October.  While  several  have  opened  since,  very  few  
-can  take  ocean  going  vessels.  UNRRA  has  had,  therefore,  to  rely  largely  
on  Shanghai  (a  single  port  for  the  relief  of  a  sub-continent),  where,  even  
at  this  early  stage  of  shipments,  there  is  an  acute  shortage  of  warehouse  
space.  
But  beyond  the  ports,  UNRRA  faced  an  even  more  baffling  problem—  
key  to  the  provision  of  relief  of  every  kind.  The  complete  breakdown  of  
inland  transportation  prevented  delivery  even  of  such  supplies  as,  by  year’s  
end,  were  available.  

## [PDF page 21]
China  needs  tremendous  amounts  of  medical  supplies.  But  again  a  
serious  conditioning  factor  is  the  dearth  of  doctors.  According  to  a  Chinese  
authority,  China  has  only  some  12,000  doctors.  She  needs  275,000.  The  
amount  of  medical  relief  supplies  must  necessarily  bear  some  relation  to  
the  numbers  of  those  qualified  to  use  them.  UNRRA  has  provided  a  
nuclear  staff  of  26  doctors,  17  nurses,  5  sanitation  officers,  to  give  advice  
and  all  possible  assistance  to  CNRRA’s  staff.  
The  first  relief  ships  moved  into  China  ports.  Four  sailed  from  the  
Western  Hemisphere  in  October,  8  in  November,  13  in  December.  
Shipments  in  December  (mostly  food  and  medical  supplies)  amounted  to  
97,046  gross  long  tons.  In  mid-December  seven  1,000-bed  hospitals  had  
been  procured  from  Far  Eastern  U.  S.  army  surpluses  and  two  new  500-bed  
hospitals  were  ready  for  shipment.  Cumulative  shipments  for  the  year  
were  197,112  tons.  Relief  was  under  way,  but  nowhere  is  the  excess  of  
need  over  the  power  to  answer  it  more  cruelly  exemplified.

Victims  of  a  peculiarly  tragic  fate  are  the  so-called  displaced  persons  of  
Europe  and  the  Far  East.  During  the  war,  millions  of  men,  women,  and  
children  were  torn  from  their  homes  and  scattered  like  chaff  across  three  
continents,  either  as  refugees  or  as  impressed  slave  laborers  of  the  Axis  
powers.  In  the  three  western  zones  of  occupied  Germany  alone,  they  
numbered  over  6  million.  Hundreds  of  thousands  were  found  in  Italy  
and  Austria,  thousands  more  in  Albania,  Greece,  the  Dodecanese  Islands,  
Egypt,  Palestine,  Cyprus,  Ethiopia,  the  Belgian  Congo,  Tanganyika,  in  
China,  and  the  Philippines.  In  enemy  territory,  once  their  usefulness  as  
slave  laborers  ceased,  they  were  left  to  fend  for  themselves.  Many  were

neighbors  or  of  their  own  governments,  for  they  were  far  from  home.
